Computational tools are increasingly commonplace in modern palaeontology. From cleaning datasets to running complex analyses, software underpins much of what we do.

This module introduces you to [palaeoverse](https://palaeoverse.palaeoverse.org), an R package developed to help you get your palaeontological data ready for analyses and to keep your code clear.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you will be able to:

- Install and load **palaeoverse**, and locate its documentation, vignettes, and further resources
- Understand the design and potential applications of **palaeoverse**
- Apply **palaeoverse** functions to explore, prepare, and visualise fossil occurrence data
- Identify **palaeoverse** functions for use in your own research workflow

## Prerequisites

### Knowledge

You should be comfortable with basic R (data frames, functions, installing packages). Experience with fossil occurrence data, for example from the [Paleobiology Database (PBDB)](https://paleobiodb.org/#/), would also be helpful but is not required.

If needed, you can refer to our [R Basics](https://palaeoverse.org/modules/pr-preview/pr-31/training/modules/R/index.html) module.

### Installation

For this module, you will need to install the following packages:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
install.packages("palaeoverse")
```
:::


> All of the example code provided runs using the in-built **palaeoverse** datasets, although we encourage you to also try out these functions on your own data.

## Module structure

This module is designed to get you up and running with **palaeoverse** as quickly as possible and includes the following:

- [Introduction to palaeoverse](introduction.qmd): Learn the core concepts behind the **palaeoverse** package, and explore the functions available to use.
- [Tutorial 1: Phanerozoic reefs](phanerozoic-reefs.qmd): Investigate latitudinal trends in Phanerozoic reefs.
- [Tutorial 2: Tetrapod biodiversity](tetrapod-biodiversity.qmd): Explore alpha diversity and geographic range size in Carboniferous and Permian tetrapods.
